headline: Education Secretary’s Manchester visit puts New Hampshire voucher debate in spotlight
dek: Linda McMahon promoted school-choice programs during an Oct. 15 tour, while Manchester families and public-school advocates warned that vouchers can strain districts already facing budget pressure.
body: U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon brought the national school-choice debate to Manchester on Thursday, touring public and private schools and meeting with New Hampshire families who disagree about how education dollars should follow students. The visit was part of McMahon’s “Returning Education to the States Tour,” a 50-state effort that the [New Hampshire Public Radio report](https://www.nhpr.org/education/2026-10-15/doe-linda-mcmahon-manchester-school-choice-vouchers) said is intended to highlight local approaches that other communities could adopt.

McMahon visited Manchester School of Technology, Southside Middle School, St. Joseph Regional Junior High School and Trinity High School before joining a parent-and-student roundtable, according to [NH Journal’s account of the visit](https://nhjournal.com/in-manchester-ed-secretary-mcmahon-makes-the-case-for-choice/). New Hampshire Education Commissioner Caitlin Davis joined the secretary for parts of the tour. The itinerary put a technical high school, a traditional public middle school and two Catholic schools in the same conversation about what families need from K–12 education.

At the roundtable, supporters described New Hampshire’s Education Freedom Account program as a practical way to pay for options that a district assignment may not provide. NHPR reported that families connected to Trinity and St. Joseph said the accounts helped with tuition and school supplies. Student Andrew Garand, whose siblings also attend Trinity, said the program supports his faith-based education and access to teachers, counselors and future college-credit classes.

The program is not a universal tuition voucher. The [New Hampshire Department of Education’s parent guide](https://www.education.nh.gov/sites/g/files/ehbemt326/files/inline-documents/sonh/nhdoe-resource-guide.pdf) says Education Freedom Accounts are state-funded grants for eligible students and can pay for qualifying expenses such as private-school tuition, tutoring, online learning and educational materials. The guide describes an income ceiling of 350% of the federal poverty level, while the amount available to an individual student can vary with the state’s per-pupil adequacy grant and qualifying additional aid.

McMahon also used the Manchester stop to promote a newer federal initiative. The U.S. Department of Education and Treasury say the Education Freedom Tax Credit allows taxpayers to claim a federal credit of up to $1,700 for contributions to scholarship-granting organizations, which can then support qualified K–12 expenses. The federal [fact sheet](https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/us-departments-education-and-treasury-release-joint-fact-sheet-historic-education-freedom-tax-credit) says the expenses can include private-school tuition, tutoring at a public school and services for students with disabilities. States must opt in for families and organizations to participate.

New Hampshire’s existing program is expanding at the same time that districts are being asked to accommodate students who use it. The [New Hampshire Bulletin reported](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/12/public-school-districts-reminded-to-accept-efa-recipients-for-free/) that a state Department of Education advisory reminded districts that, beginning this school year, EFA recipients may take classes, join sports teams and participate in clubs and extracurricular programs at their resident public school without paying an additional fee, unless the district determines it is at capacity. Supporters call that flexibility empowering; public-school advocates say districts may have to provide services without receiving a matching reimbursement.

That tension was visible outside the private-school roundtable. NHPR reported that Southside Middle School parent Christina Goodwin criticized vouchers as a way to direct taxpayer money toward private education while public schools continue to educate most New Hampshire children. Her objection came as Manchester works through school-budget pressures and long-deferred middle-school renovations. NHPR also noted that a ballot question on the city’s school-budget tax cap was approaching, making education funding an especially immediate issue for local voters.

The visit therefore offered no resolution to the underlying dispute. McMahon argued that more options give parents greater control and said New Hampshire provides a model for other states. Critics questioned whether accounts broaden opportunity or shift public resources away from district schools. New Hampshire families will see the practical effects in classrooms, extracurricular programs and household budgets, while lawmakers and voters continue to decide how much education funding should remain in district systems and how much should be directed through alternative providers.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: McMahon’s Manchester visit spotlights New Hampshire school choice debate
seoDescription: Education Secretary Linda McMahon promoted school choice during an Oct. 15 Manchester visit as New Hampshire families debated vouchers and public-school funding.
